newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean leader Frei to talk trade on U.S. visit.
newsitem.headline: Chilean leader Frei to talk trade on U.S. visit.

text.p: Chilean President Eduardo Frei begins a four-day visit to the United States on Monday aimed at boosting trade, although the vexed issue of Chile's long-delayed entry to NAFTA will not top the agenda.
Frei will be the first foreign leader to make an official visit to Washington since President Bill Clinton began his second term in January.
Frei will hold talks with Clinton and address Congress.
Chilean officials said Frei will focus on broad political and trade issues, playing down Chile's frustrated bid to join the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).
"This visit has multiple objectives," said Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat, one of four ministers who will accompany Frei.
"It will be more of a political and institutional agenda than just trade, but trade will of course be included."
Frei's talks with Clinton at the White House on Wednesday will include Chile's role in the U.N Security Council and the next Americas Summit, which will be held in Santiago in 1998.

Chile will broach the thorny issue of fruit exporters' demands for compensation for losses caused by a U.S. ban on Chilean fruit imports in 1989 after a grape poisoning scare, Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza said.
"As long as we are not satisfied with the solution to the grapes problem, we will keep bringing up the issue," he said.
Insulza said Frei will not discuss Clinton's difficulties in obtaining "fast track" authority from Congress to negotiate trade accords, which stalled Chile's NAFTA bid last year.
Chile has refused to enter NAFTA talks until the Clinton administration gets this authority because it fears Congress would undo any accord under pressure from lobby groups.
Chile was invited to join the North American trade bloc, which links the United States, Canada and Mexico, at the first Summit of the Americas in Miami more than two years ago.
For Chilean businessmen the deal with NAFTA has lost much of its urgency as Chile has recently signed trade accords with Canada and the Mercosur trade bloc.

"NAFTA doesn't have the same degree of importance it had two or three years ago as Chile has moved ahead with other bilateral agreements and its economy has continued to grow," said Alex Fernandez, president of the Chilean-U.S. Chamber of Commerce.
Bilateral trade has soared in recent years to over $5 billion in 1996. The United States is one of the most important markets for Chilean salmon, wine and fresh fruit.
U.S. companies are among the chief foreign investors in Chile with billions of dollars invested, mainly in mining.
